title: Hearts at rest
hook: in the remembrance of Allah hearts find rest (13:28)

segments.voice: Yesterday, change what is in yourselves, and your line was change starts inside. Did you catch the inner habit, and try the new thought? Day four hundred forty-four.

It's late. The house is quiet, the phone is face down, and your mind is doing laps. The email you didn't answer. The thing someone said at lunch. The bill. Back to the email. You know the feeling of a heart that won't settle: not broken, not in crisis, just restless, like a glass of water that keeps getting bumped. Surah ar-Ra'd has a verse for that. Many Muslims can recite it from memory, and it's written in calligraphy on walls and in cars. It's short, and it doesn't promise that the email goes away.

Verse twenty-eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Who have believed and whose hearts have rest in the remembrance of Allah. Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" The key word is tatma'innu, find rest. It comes from itmi'nan, a settled calm, the stillness of something that has stopped shaking: the same root as the soul at rest at the end of Surah al-Fajr, which you met last year. The same word appears in al-Baqarah, when Ibrahim asks God to show him how He gives life to the dead. God asks: do you not believe? And Ibrahim says: yes, but so that my heart may be at rest. Even a prophet wanted that settling. And the means is dhikr, remembrance. Dhikr is the word for calling God to mind: in the prayer, in reading the Qur'an, and in short phrases repeated through the day. Subhanallah, glory be to God. Alhamdulillah, praise belongs to God. La ilaha illallah, no god but God. Notice the shape of the verse. It says the remembrance of Allah twice, and in the second half the Arabic puts those words first, before the verb: it is in God's remembrance, and there, that hearts find rest. Commentators read that order as emphasis: there, and not elsewhere. Another verse adds a promise that runs both ways: remember Me, and I will remember you. And a hadith in Bukhari puts it starkly: the one who remembers his Lord and the one who doesn't are like the living and the dead. The verse doesn't say the world calms down. It says the heart can. The glass can stop shaking, even while the table is still being bumped.
screen: `TATMA'INNU — A SETTLED CALM.` · `IBRAHIM: THAT MY HEART MAY REST.` · `DHIKR — CALLING GOD TO MIND.` · `THERE, HEARTS FIND REST.` · then, large: `HEARTS REST IN REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: two minutes of dhikr. Sit comfortably, and let the breath slow. If you pray, choose one short phrase, subhanallah, or alhamdulillah, or la ilaha illallah, and repeat it quietly with the breath, counting on your fingers if that helps. If you'd rather not, choose one word that brings you to stillness, and return to it each time your mind wanders off to the email. Wandering is fine. Coming back is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Hearts at rest. 13:28: in the remembrance of God, hearts find rest, itmi'nan, the stillness of something that has stopped shaking. Today's word.
Your line: hearts rest in remembering. Tonight, when your mind starts doing laps, try the phrase or the word from today, ten times, slowly. Day four hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims practice dhikr after the daily prayers and through the day, repeating phrases such as subhanallah, alhamdulillah and la ilaha illallah, often counting on the fingers or on prayer beads; Sufi orders also gather for dhikr together.

original.note: Arabic: "hearts find rest" (13:28), from itmi'nan, a settled calm.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer makes you feel better.
what it means: remembering God settles the heart, even while the world stays loud.
what a scholar hears: in 13:28's second clause, bi-dhikri llahi is placed before the verb, which grammarians read as restriction or emphasis; the same root appears in Ibrahim's request in 2:260.
